doc_description: Square, Inc.’s 2020 Form 10-K (filed Feb 23, 2021) covering its shift to two segments (Seller and Cash App), COVID-19 effects including facilitation of about $857M in PPP loans, surging Cash App bitcoin revenue of $4.57B (driving total net revenue to $9.50B on $103.7B GPV and 36M+ monthly actives), substantial convertible note financings, and extensive risk, regulatory, and controls disclosures.

structure.title: Preface
structure.summary:
- SEC filing: Square, Inc.’s Annual Report on Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2020 (Commission File No. 001-37622).
- Company and securities details: Delaware corporation; principal office in San Francisco, CA; Class A common stock (ticker: SQ) listed on the NYSE; registrant phone number; IRS Employer Identification Number.
- Filer status and compliance: Well-known seasoned issuer; large accelerated filer; not a shell company; confirms timely filing of required reports and submission of Interactive Data Files; auditor attestation of internal control over financial reporting (SOX 404(b)).
- Market and share data: Approximate market value of non-affiliate equity as of June 30, 2020 ($38.7 billion); shares outstanding as of February 18, 2021 for Class A and Class B stock.
- Incorporation by reference: Portions of the Definitive Proxy Statement for the Annual Meeting incorporated into Part III.
- Table of contents overview: Parts I–IV covering Business; Risk Factors; Properties; Legal Proceedings; Market information; Selected Financial Data; MD&A; Market Risk; Financial Statements; Controls and Procedures; and other standard 10-K items.
- Forward-looking statements: Cautionary note outlining risks and uncertainties, including impacts of COVID-19, transaction and loan losses, PPP participation and liquidity effects, growth strategies and product development, expected benefits of products, GPV and revenue expectations (Seller and Cash App), product launches and acquisitions, IP, litigation, tax positions, share-based compensation, accounting guidance, restricted cash, and liquidity; no obligation to update.
- Business overview: Purpose of economic empowerment; evolution from enabling card acceptance (founded 2009) to offering 30+ products and services; effective June 30, 2020 reporting structure changed to two reportable segments—Seller and Cash App.
- Seller ecosystem: Integrated software, hardware, and financial services helping sellers start, run, and grow businesses; emphasis on cohesive, self-serve, digital tools and cross-sell; 2020 metrics include $103.7 billion GPV, over 2 billion card payments from 405 million cards, 210+ million buyer profiles, and ~295 million items listed.
- Cash App ecosystem: Suite of financial services aiming to make money management accessible—expanding from peer-to-peer payments to storing, sending, receiving, spending, and investing.

structure.summary:
- Overview of Square’s origin (founded in 2009 to enable sellers to accept card payments) and evolution into offering 30+ products and services for businesses, alongside building Cash App for individuals.
- Mission centered on economic empowerment guiding product development across both ecosystems.
- Shift in reporting structure effective June 30, 2020, from one to two reportable segments: Seller and Cash App, aligned with how management and the CODM assess performance.
- Seller Ecosystem: an integrated commerce platform combining software, hardware, and financial services; positioned against a fragmented industry by offering cohesive, fast, self-serve, elegant solutions.

- Cash App Ecosystem: a suite of financial services helping individuals manage money; evolved from simple peer-to-peer transfers to enabling users to store, send, receive, spend, and invest, with a goal to make money more relatable, instant, and accessible.

structure.title: Business
structure.heading: Item 1. Business
structure.start_phrase: We started Square in February 2009 to enable businesses (sellers) to accept card payments, an important capability that was previously inaccessible tomany businesses.
structure.summary:
- Company overview and segmentation: Origins of Square (2009), purpose of economic empowerment, expansion to two reportable segments as of June 30, 2020—Seller and Cash App—reflecting distinct ecosystems and management reporting.
- Seller ecosystem: Cohesive suite of 30+ software, hardware, and financial services enabling sellers to start, run, and grow businesses; emphasis on integrated, self-serve, omnichannel tools and efficient cross-sell. 2020 metrics: $103.7B GPV from 2B+ card payments and 405M cards; 210M buyer profiles; ~295M items listed; rising mix of larger sellers (60% of Q4 2020 GPV).
- Seller software: POS (Square Point of Sale, Appointments, Retail, Restaurants), online commerce (Square Online, Online Checkout, Invoices, Virtual Terminal), CRM and operations (Team Management, Contracts, Loyalty, Marketing, Gift Cards, Feedback, Dashboard); monetization via transaction, subscription, and service fees; developer platform with Payment and Commerce APIs/SDKs.
- Seller hardware: Magstripe reader, Contactless and Chip reader, Square Stand, Register, and Terminal; compatibility with major card networks and accessories.
- Seller financial services: Managed Payments (settlement, disputes, PCI), Risk Manager, Instant Transfer, Square Card (prepaid debit; interchange revenue), Square Capital (data-driven loan facilitation including PPP; forward-flow funding), Square Payroll; plan to launch Square Financial Services (ILC) in 2021, pending regulatory approval.
- Cash App ecosystem: Consumer financial services enabling storing, sending, receiving, spending, and investing; strong brand and simple UX; serves primarily the U.S., with some European services.
- Cash App products: P2P transfers, stored balances (approx. $2.0B as of 12/31/2020), direct deposit (routing/account numbers), cross-border U.S.–U.K. payments; Cash Card debit with Boost rewards (interchange revenue); investing in stocks/ETFs (including fractional) and bitcoin (revenue recognized on customer bitcoin purchases); addition of tax filing via acquisition of Credit Karma Tax.
- Cash App scale and engagement: 36M+ monthly transacting actives as of Dec 2020; top-ranked finance app by U.S. downloads in 2020.
- COVID-19 response: Fee waivers and subscription pauses for sellers; acceleration of omnichannel features (online, curbside, delivery, eGift Cards); free marketing campaigns; facilitation of ~$857M PPP loans to 80k+ small businesses. For Cash App: education on CARES Act, expanded direct deposit for government funds, Boost adaptations to pandemic-relevant categories.
- Customers and markets: Diverse seller base by industry, size, and geography (U.S., Canada, Japan, Australia, U.K.); no single customer >5% of GPV or revenue in 2018–2020. Cash App customers across all 50 states and nearly every U.S. county; presence in Europe.
- Sales and marketing: Strong brands; Seller NPS ~65; acquisition via direct marketing, PR, direct sales for larger sellers, and >700 partners via App Marketplace; scalable in-product communication. Cash App growth led by P2P network effects, referrals, paid advertising, partnerships, and feature launches.
- Product development and technology: Cross-platform, rapid release cadence, scalable infrastructure, heavy use of data science/ML (automated risk >99.95% of transactions); in-house hardware design with third-party manufacturing.
- Competition: Seller ecosystem competes with manual processes, business software vendors, payment terminal providers, merchant acquirers, banks, payroll processors, and alternative lenders; differentiation via integrated ecosystem, UX, transparent pricing, and innovation. Cash App competes with P2P apps, debit/prepaid offerings, rewards programs, brokerages, and crypto services; competes on brand and simplicity.
- Human capital: 5,477 full-time employees (662 outside U.S.) as of Dec 31, 2020; purpose-driven culture, remote-work flexibility, learning and manager training, inclusion and diversity focus (public reporting), competitive total rewards and annual pay equity analyses.
- Intellectual property: Protection via contracts, trademarks, copyrights, domains, trade secrets, and patents; ongoing patent program; use of some licensed/open-source technology.
- Government and regulatory environment: Extensive U.S. and international compliance across payments licensing (money transmission, MSB registration), consumer protection, AML, bank regulation (FDIC/Utah approvals for ILC), broker-dealer rules for Cash App Investing (SEC/FINRA/state), virtual currency (NY BitLicense) and potential additional licensing; privacy/data protection; communications laws; other evolving regulatory areas.
- Seasonality and revenue mix: Seller transaction revenue typically strongest in Q4; Cash App seasonality tied to government funds and tax refunds; 2020 results skewed by significant bitcoin revenue (48% of total net revenue; 85% of revenue increase), which depends on demand and market price.
- Corporate and investor information: Incorporation (Delaware, 2009), headquarters (San Francisco), websites and investor relations resources, use of social media for disclosures, availability of SEC filings and governance documents; trademark notes.

structure.title: Risk Factors
structure.heading: Item 1A. Risk Factors
structure.start_phrase: Investing in our securities involves a high degree of risk.
structure.summary:
- Item 1A (Risk Factors) from a Form 10-K, warning that investing in the company’s securities involves significant risk; if these risks materialize, operations and the Class A common stock price could be materially harmed.
- Summarizes three main categories of risks:
  - Business and industry risks: ongoing COVID-19 impacts and participation in related government relief programs; brand protection; retention and growth of sellers and Cash App users; ability to invest while maintaining profitability; product and market expansion; rapid innovation needs in payments/financial services; intense competition; international growth; M&A and other strategic transactions; and Square Capital-specific risks around funding availability, seller repayments, bank partnerships, and product expansion.
  - Operational risks: data privacy and security (misuse, unauthorized access, disclosure); security breaches and human error; system failures, service interruptions, and catastrophic events; bitcoin custody risks (private keys, hacks, data loss); effectiveness of risk management; reliance on payment card networks and acquiring processors; dependence on third-party providers for processing and settlement; reliance on key management and talent; strength of internal controls and systems; integration with multiple operating systems and hardware interoperability; component shortages, tariffs, pricing and supply changes; and demand forecasting and inventory management.
  - Economic, financial, and tax risks: deteriorating macroeconomic conditions; higher-than-expected tax liabilities or valuation allowances on deferred tax assets; limited or costly access to financing and restrictive covenants; ability to service convertible senior notes; and counterparty risk related to convertible note hedge transactions.

nodes.summary:
This excerpt is the Risk Factors section (Item 1A) of a Form 10-K, summarizing key risks that could materially affect the company’s business, financial results, and stock price. It groups risks into three areas: 
- Business/industry risks: impacts from COVID-19 and related relief programs; brand protection; retaining and growing sellers and Cash App users; sustaining profitability amid investment; product and market expansion; rapid innovation in payments/financial services; competition; global expansion; M&A and other strategic transactions; and specific Square Capital risks around funding availability, seller repayments, bank partnerships, and product expansion. 
- Operational risks: data privacy/security incidents; system outages and catastrophic events; custody and security of bitcoin, including private key access; effectiveness of risk management; dependence on card networks, acquiring processors, and other third-party providers; reliance on key leaders and broader talent retention; robustness of internal controls; technical integration across operating systems and third-party devices; supply chain constraints, tariffs, and component changes; and demand forecasting and inventory management. 
- Economic/financial/tax risks: macroeconomic deterioration; higher-than-expected tax liabilities or deferred tax asset valuation allowances; limited or costly access to financing and restrictive covenants; servicing obligations on convertible senior notes; and counterparty risk tied to convertible note hedge transactions.

nodes.title: Risk Factors Summary
nodes.heading: 1.1 Risk Factors Summary
nodes.start_phrase: Our business operations are subject to numerous risks and uncertainties, including those outside of our control, that could cause our actual results to be harmed, including risks regarding the following:
nodes.summary:
- This excerpt is Item 1A. Risk Factors from an annual Form 10-K, warning that investing involves a high degree of risk and that adverse events could materially affect the business and stock price.
- It presents a Risk Factors Summary organized into five categories:
  - Risks related to business and industry: ongoing COVID-19 impacts and participation in government relief programs; brand protection; ability to retain and grow sellers and Cash App customers; investment needs vs. profitability; product and market expansion; pace of innovation in payments/financial services; competitive pressures; global expansion; M&A and other strategic transactions; and Square Capital-specific risks (capital availability, seller repayments, bank partnership structure, product expansion).
  - Operational risks: data misuse or unauthorized access; security breaches and human error; system failures and catastrophic events; custody risks for bitcoin (private keys, hacks, data loss); adequacy of risk management; dependence on card networks and acquiring processors; reliance on third-party processors and settlement partners; dependence on key personnel and talent retention; effectiveness of internal controls; integration with operating systems and third-party devices; component shortages, tariffs, delays, or discontinuations; and demand forecasting and inventory management.
  - Economic, financial, and tax risks: macroeconomic deterioration; higher-than-expected tax liabilities or valuation allowances; limited or costly financing and covenant constraints; ability to service convertible senior notes; and counterparty risk related to convertible note hedge transactions.
  - Legal, regulatory, and compliance risks: extensive regulation across operations; evolving privacy and data protection rules; money transmitter obligations; regulation and scrutiny of Square Financial Services (Utah industrial bank) including source-of-strength requirements; regulation of Cash App Investing (SEC/FINRA) and net capital rules; potential FINRA-imposed business practice changes; litigation and government investigations; intellectual property protection challenges; and volatility/impairment risks tied to bitcoin investments.
  - Risks related to ownership of common stock: dual-class share structure; Class A stock price volatility; impacts of convertible note hedge and warrant transactions; anti-takeover provisions in charter/bylaws and Delaware law; and exclusive forum bylaw provisions.
- The section then expands on COVID-19-specific risks: significant macroeconomic uncertainty; outsized impact on small-business sellers; effects of government restrictions (lockdowns, travel bans) driving unemployment and reduced spending; operational disruptions (e.g., reduced Cash App support due to vendor shutdowns); shifts to remote work and curtailed travel/events; and high uncertainty around duration, vaccine efficacy/distribution, and recovery timeline, with potential lasting impacts such as tighter credit, customer insolvencies, and recessionary pressures.

nodes.title: Risks Related to Our Business and Our Industry
nodes.heading: 1.2 Risks Related to Our Business and Our Industry
nodes.start_phrase: Global health concerns relating to the COVID-19 pandemic and related government actions taken to reduce the spread of the virus have been weighing on the macroeconomic environment,
nodes.summary:
- Legal, regulatory, and compliance risks: broad oversight across the business; evolving privacy and data protection obligations; licensed money transmitter requirements; regulation of Square Financial Services (Utah industrial bank) including “source of financial strength” obligations; regulation of Cash App Investing (SEC-registered, FINRA member) including net capital and other capital rules and potential FINRA-driven business practice changes; exposure to litigation, government investigations, and IP disputes; challenges protecting IP; and volatility, impairment, and loss risks tied to bitcoin holdings.
- Risks related to ownership of common stock: dual-class share structure; volatility of Class A stock; effects of convertible note hedge and warrant transactions; anti-takeover provisions in charter, bylaws, and Delaware law; and exclusive forum bylaw provisions.
- Business and industry risks focused on COVID-19: macroeconomic deterioration affecting small business sellers; government restrictions reducing consumer and business spending; operational disruptions (e.g., reduced Cash App customer support due to vendor shutdowns); shifts to remote work and curtailed travel/events; high uncertainty regarding duration, severity, vaccine impact, and recovery; and potential lasting adverse effects including tighter credit, customer bankruptcies/insolvencies, and recession, all of which may materially impact operations, results, and financial condition.

nodes.title: The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic and measures intended to prevent its spread have had, and may continue to have, a material and adverse effect on our business and results of operations.
nodes.heading: 1.2.1 The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic and measures intended to prevent its spread have had, and may continue to have, a material and adverse effect on our business and results of operations.
nodes.start_phrase: Global health concerns relating to the COVID-19 pandemic and related government actions taken to reduce the spread of the virus have been weighing on the macroeconomic environment,
nodes.summary:
- Highlights extensive legal, regulatory, and compliance exposure across the business, including privacy and data protection, money transmitter obligations, and oversight of key subsidiaries: Square Financial Services (a Utah industrial bank with “source of financial strength” obligations) and Cash App Investing (SEC-registered, FINRA member with net capital and other requirements), as well as potential FINRA-driven changes to business practices.
- Notes litigation risks (including intellectual property claims, government investigations, and regulatory disputes), challenges protecting IP, and volatility/impairment risk tied to bitcoin investments.
- Outlines ownership-related risks: dual-class share structure, Class A stock price volatility, impacts of convertible note hedge and warrant transactions, anti-takeover provisions in corporate documents and Delaware law, and exclusive forum bylaw provisions.
- Details COVID-19 impacts: macroeconomic weakness and uncertainty, disproportionate harm to small-business sellers, operational disruptions (e.g., reduced customer support capacity, remote work, travel and event restrictions), and the unpredictable duration, severity, and aftereffects (credit availability, bankruptcies, recession).
- Describes participation in government relief programs, especially PPP lending via Square Capital (including second-draw eligibility, two- or five-year 1% loans, forgiveness criteria), with approximately $857 million facilitated by December 31, 2020; mix of retained and participated loans, and Federal Reserve borrowing secured by PPP loans; plans to continue participating.
- Explains PPP-related risks: evolving and untested program requirements; potential errors in documentation, verification, forgiveness, and servicing; risk of SBA denying guarantees or forgiveness; underwriting scrutiny; potential losses, litigation, and reputational harm.
- Covers facilitation of stimulus and unemployment payments through Cash App (direct deposit via account/routing numbers, cash-in from state prepaid cards, expanded direct deposit eligibility), and associated heightened risks of fraud, data breaches, technical issues, and resulting operational, compliance, legal, reputational, and governmental enforcement exposure.

nodes.title: Our participation in government relief programs set up in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, such as facilitating loans to businesses under the Paycheck Protection Program or unemployment benefits and stimulus payments to individuals through Cash App, may subject us to new risks and uncertainties.
nodes.heading: 1.2.2 Our participation in government relief programs set up in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, such as facilitating loans to businesses under the Paycheck Protection Program or unemployment benefits and stimulus payments to individuals through Cash App, may subject us to new risks and uncertainties.
nodes.start_phrase: Federal, state, local, and foreign governmental authorities have enacted, and may enact in the future, legislation, regulations, and programs in response to the COVID-19 pandemic intended to provide economic relief to businesses and individuals.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of COVID-19-related risk factors, noting potential material impacts on operations and the amplification of known risks due to participation in government relief programs.
- Square Capital’s role in the Paycheck Protection Program (PPP): approved participant status; program extension to March 31, 2021 with an additional $284B; loan terms (1% fixed rate; two- or five-year terms; up to 2.5x payroll, or 3.5x for qualifying restaurants); forgiveness criteria (use on eligible expenses, at least 60% for payroll, employment maintenance).
- Second-draw PPP eligibility: fewer than 300 employees, at least a 25% revenue decline in any 2020 quarter vs. the same 2019 quarter, and full use of the first PPP loan.
- Operational footprint and funding: approximately $857M in PPP loans facilitated as of December 31, 2020; mix of retained loans and sold participations; borrowing from the Federal Reserve secured by PPP loans; plans to retain second-round PPP loans and continue accessing Fed funding.
- PPP-related risks: evolving and untested processes; documentation, verification, forgiveness, and servicing challenges; exposure if the SBA declines guarantees or forgiveness due to errors or noncompliance; heightened scrutiny of underwriting and documentation; potential losses, litigation, and reputational harm; possible negative impact on business and results.
- Cash App’s facilitation of federal stimulus and unemployment payments: enabling direct deposits via account/routing numbers, accepting deposits from state-issued prepaid cards, and working with partner banks to expand direct deposit eligibility.
- Risks from facilitating stimulus/unemployment payments: increased susceptibility to fraud, data breaches, and technical issues due to rapid, complex program implementation; resulting operational, compliance, legal, and reputational risks, with potential for governmental action, litigation, and material adverse losses.

nodes.title: Our business depends on a strong and trusted brand, and any failure to maintain, protect, and enhance our brand would hurt our business.
nodes.heading: 1.2.3 Our business depends on a strong and trusted brand, and any failure to maintain, protect, and enhance our brand would hurt our business.
nodes.start_phrase: We have developed a strong and trusted brand that has contributed significantly to the success of our business.
nodes.summary:
- Emphasis on the critical importance of maintaining, protecting, and enhancing a strong, trusted brand to drive adoption, retention, and growth.
- Risks that product, feature, privacy, or terms changes could alienate customers and damage brand equity; brand marketing may not deliver adequate ROI.
- Dependence on third-party advertising platforms (e.g., Google, Twitter, Facebook) and retail partners for visibility, customer acquisition, and hardware sales; adverse platform changes or inability to maintain partnerships could harm growth and increase costs.
- Multiple potential sources of brand harm: service quality failures, data protection lapses or misuse, third-party fraud, compliance failures, litigation, partner or provider misconduct, misinformation/negative publicity, and regulatory or policy controversies.
- Recognition that revenue growth has slowed at times and may slow or decline further; growth rates may differ between reporting segments, with Cash App and Seller potentially growing at different paces.
- Customer retention risk due to lack of long-term contracts and relatively low switching costs; usage may drop due to satisfaction levels, pricing/competition, macroeconomic conditions, or reduced end-customer spending (including impacts from events like COVID-19).
- Growth strategy hinges on retaining and expanding usage among existing sellers and Cash App customers, acquiring new customers (including larger sellers), and successfully launching innovative products and services.
- Importance of increasing Cash App monthly transacting active customers and deepening their engagement as a key driver of long-term financial performance.

nodes.title: As our revenue has increased, our growth rate has slowed at times in the past and may slow or decline in the future, and our growth rates in each of our reporting segments may vary. Future revenue growth depends on our ability to retain existing sellers, attract new sellers, and increase sales to both new and existing sellers, as well as our ability to attract and retain Cash App customers and grow their use of Cash App services.
nodes.heading: 1.2.4 As our revenue has increased, our growth rate has slowed at times in the past and may slow or decline in the future, and our growth rates in each of our reporting segments may vary. Future revenue growth depends on our ability to retain existing sellers, attract new sellers, and increase sales to both new and existing sellers, as well as our ability to attract and retain Cash App customers and grow their use of Cash App services.
nodes.start_phrase: Our rate of revenue growth has slowed at times in the past and may decline in the future,
nodes.summary:
- Emphasis on the critical importance of maintaining a strong, trusted brand; risks that changes to products, features, privacy practices, or terms could alienate customers; brand marketing may be costly and ineffective.
- Dependence on third-party advertising platforms (e.g., Google, Twitter, Facebook) and retail partners for visibility and customer acquisition; changes in platform operations, pricing, data-use policies, or partnership terms could hinder marketing and growth.
- Multiple potential sources of brand harm: service or quality failures (by the company or partners), data protection lapses or misuse, third-party fraud, compliance failures, litigation, partner misconduct, misinformation, negative publicity, handling of customer complaints, product changes, and privacy/security issues.
- Slowing or variable revenue growth across segments; reliance on retaining and expanding existing sellers and Cash App customers and attracting new ones; lack of long-term contracts and low switching costs heighten churn risk; macroeconomic factors (including COVID-19 impacts) can reduce seller activity and revenue.
- Growth depends on deeper engagement and successful product innovation; Cash App monthly active customer growth is essential but volatile and influenced by network effects, technical issues, customer support, fraud/scams, and reputation; growth spikes tied to external events (e.g., government stimulus) may be unsustainable; bitcoin price volatility can distort Cash App revenue trends.
- Profitability risk despite some profitable years; history of net losses and accumulated deficit; plans for substantial ongoing investments (people, marketing, product development, acquisitions, infrastructure, international expansion, and compliance) may increase expenses; upfront costs to acquire/support sellers vs. deferred revenues can pressure margins; strategic long-term decisions may hurt short-term results and may not deliver expected benefits.
- Risks in expanding product portfolio and entering new markets: new offerings may not gain adoption or generate meaningful revenue; limited experience in newer markets; technological, operational, and regulatory challenges (including potential service disruptions) could harm the business.
- Specific risk from Cash App investing features (bitcoin, stocks, ETFs): customer losses from market volatility could drive churn and damage brand and reputation; newer initiatives may not recoup investments, require significant management attention, and could limit growth.

nodes.title: We have generated significant net losses in the past, and we intend to continue to invest substantially in our business. Thus, we may not be able to maintain profitability.
nodes.heading: 1.2.5 We have generated significant net losses in the past, and we intend to continue to invest substantially in our business. Thus, we may not be able to maintain profitability.
nodes.start_phrase: While we generated net income of $213.1 million and $375.4 million for the years ended December 31, 2020 and 2019, respectively, we generated net losses of $38.5 million for the year ended December 31, 2018.
nodes.summary:
- Cash App user growth has been volatile and may slow or decline due to factors such as product innovation challenges, network effects, technical issues, inadequate support, fraud/scams, and brand harm; stimulus-driven surges may be unsustainable, and bitcoin price movements can distort reported revenue relative to engagement.
- Continued investment in the Square platform to add or improve features may not succeed; unsuccessful initiatives could slow or reduce growth.
- Profitability is uncertain: despite recent net income, the company has an accumulated deficit and plans substantial ongoing investments (hiring, sales/marketing, product development, acquisitions, infrastructure, international expansion, and compliance) that could raise expenses faster than revenue.
- Costs to acquire/support new or larger sellers and Cash App customers, including higher third-party advertising fees, may increase significantly; upfront seller costs versus deferred revenue recognition can lead to near-term losses.
- The company may make decisions that hurt short-term results in pursuit of long-term benefits, which may not meet investor expectations or materialize, potentially harming the business.
- Efforts to broaden products and services and enter new markets may fail to generate or sustain revenue; acceptance in new markets is uncertain.
- Offerings face technological, operational, and regulatory risks; service disruptions or failures could materially and adversely affect the business.
- Cash App investing features (bitcoin, stocks, ETFs) expose customers to market volatility; customer losses may drive churn and damage brand and reputation.
- New initiatives may not yield growth or timely returns and require significant management attention, potentially limiting growth and harming reputation.

nodes.title: Our efforts to expand our product portfolio and market reach may not succeed and may reduce our revenue growth.
nodes.heading: 1.2.6 Our efforts to expand our product portfolio and market reach may not succeed and may reduce our revenue growth.
nodes.start_phrase: While we have grown the proportion of revenue from newer products and services from each of the Cash App and Seller segments and we intend to continue to broaden the scope of products and services we offer,
nodes.summary:
- Cash App growth volatility: Monthly active/transacting customer growth has fluctuated and may slow or decline due to factors such as product innovation effectiveness, network effects, technical issues, inadequate support, fraud/scams, and reputational harm. Government stimulus can create unsustainable spikes. Bitcoin price volatility can distort Cash App revenue and decouple it from user or engagement growth.
- Profitability risk despite recent profits: The company has a history of net losses and an accumulated deficit, and plans substantial ongoing investment (hiring, sales/marketing, product development, acquisitions, infrastructure, international expansion, legal/compliance). Rising acquisition/support and advertising costs, plus upfront costs for onboarding new sellers, could increase losses if revenue growth lags or expenses aren’t controlled. Long-term strategic choices may hurt short-term results and may not deliver expected benefits.
- Product and market expansion uncertainty: Efforts to broaden products and services in Cash App and Seller segments may fail to sustain or grow revenue, especially in newer markets where the company has limited experience. Offerings carry technological, operational, and regulatory risks; service disruptions or failures could materially harm the business.
- Investment features risk: Cash App’s investing products (bitcoin, stocks, ETFs) increase accessibility but expose users to market volatility; user losses could drive churn and damage brand and reputation.
- Return on new initiatives: New activities may not produce growth or timely ROI, could consume significant management time, and may adversely affect reputation and overall business performance.

nodes.title: Our long-term success depends on our ability to develop products and services to address the rapidly evolving market for payments and financial services, and, if we are not able to implement successful enhancements and new features for our products and services, our business could be materially and adversely affected.
nodes.heading: 1.2.7 Our long-term success depends on our ability to develop products and services to address the rapidly evolving market for payments and financial services, and, if we are not able to implement successful enhancements and new features for our products and services, our business could be materially and adversely affected.
nodes.start_phrase: Rapid and significant technological changes continue to confront the industries in which we operate, including developments in omnichannel commerce, proximity payment devices (including contactless payments via NFC technology), digital banking, mobile financial apps,
nodes.summary:
- The company’s long-term success hinges on rapidly developing and enhancing products and services for an evolving payments and financial services market.
- Rapid technological change (omnichannel commerce, NFC/contactless, digital banking, mobile apps, cryptocurrencies, tokenization) may render current offerings obsolete and demands significant, timely investment.
- Development efforts may be constrained by industry standards, payment network rules, laws and regulations, customer resistance to change, and third-party intellectual property rights.
- The company depends partly on third parties—including competitors—for access to new technologies and market development; failure to anticipate or respond to industry shifts could impair the business.
- Products must interoperate with diverse systems, infrastructures, and devices and be tailored to customer needs; inability to maintain compatibility or meet requirements could reduce demand and harm customer satisfaction.
- The competitive landscape is intense and evolving, with existing and new entrants (including non-traditional payments players) introducing rival products and services.
- Many competitors have greater resources, larger customer bases, and economies of scale; mergers and acquisitions may strengthen them further.
- Long-standing exclusive relationships between sellers and competitors, and stronger brand trust in competing services, can limit customer acquisition and differentiation.
- Pricing pressures, including competitors’ cross-subsidization, may force price reductions and customized favorable terms, compressing gross profit; the company negotiates discounts and incentives with large sellers.

nodes.title: Substantial and increasingly intense competition in our industry may harm our business.
nodes.heading: 1.2.8 Substantial and increasingly intense competition in our industry may harm our business.
nodes.start_phrase: We compete in markets characterized by vigorous competition, changing technology, evolving industry standards, changing customer needs, and frequent introductions of new products and services.
nodes.summary:
- The company’s long-term success depends on continuously developing and enhancing products and services to keep pace with rapid technological change in payments and financial services.
- Emerging technologies—omnichannel commerce, contactless/NFC, digital banking, mobile financial apps, cryptocurrencies, and tokenization—could outperform or render current offerings obsolete; adopting them may require significant time and investment with uncertain returns.
- Product development may be constrained by industry standards, card network rules, evolving laws and regulations, customer resistance, and third-party intellectual property rights.
- The company relies partly on third parties, including competitors, for access to new technologies and market development; failing to anticipate or respond to industry shifts could impair the business.
- Maintaining compatibility with diverse systems, infrastructures, and devices requires continuous updates and customization; failures can reduce demand and customer satisfaction.
- The competitive landscape is intense and expected to escalate, including from non-traditional entrants; larger competitors may leverage greater resources, customer bases, and economies of scale, amplified by mergers and acquisitions.
- Long-standing or exclusive seller relationships with competitors and stronger brand trust can hinder customer acquisition; inability to differentiate would adversely affect results.
- Pricing pressures, including competitor cross-subsidization and seller demands for discounts or customized pricing, could force lower prices and increased incentives, reducing gross profit—especially as the mix shifts toward larger sellers.
- Global expansion requires substantial resources and time, with uncertain payback, and introduces risks such as local competition, cultural and language adaptation, IP and data protection challenges, third-party integration, staffing and management complexities, and higher compliance and operational costs.
- International operations add legal and regulatory burdens (payments, data privacy/protection, information security, anti-corruption/AML), trade and sanctions exposure, FX and tax complexity, public health disruptions (e.g., COVID-19), and geopolitical instability; unsuccessful expansion could limit growth.

nodes.title: Expanding our business globally could subject us to new challenges and risks.
nodes.heading: 1.2.9 Expanding our business globally could subject us to new challenges and risks.
nodes.start_phrase: We currently offer our services and products in multiple countries and plan to continue expanding our business further globally.
nodes.summary:
- Discounts and incentives used to drive product and service adoption—especially for large sellers—may need to increase, which could compress gross margins.
- The company is expanding globally, which requires significant time, resources, controls, and upfront investment with uncertain or delayed returns.
- Key global expansion risks include:
  - Difficulty attracting sufficient sellers and Cash App customers and misjudging local competitive dynamics.
  - Challenges adapting to local business customs, language, and culture, and higher costs to localize offerings.
  - Greater complexity and cost in protecting intellectual property and sensitive data.
  - Potential lack of acceptance of products/services or need to alter business practices.
  - Dependence on and integration with local third-party providers.
  - Operational hurdles in staffing and managing foreign teams, plus higher travel, infrastructure, legal, and compliance costs.
  - Recruiting and retention challenges and maintaining company culture.
  - Gaining acceptance from industry self-regulatory bodies.
  - Compliance burdens with evolving and potentially conflicting laws on payments, data privacy/protection, information security, anti-corruption/bribery/AML, and taxation across jurisdictions.
  - Exposure to tariffs, sanctions, fines, trade restrictions, and foreign exchange volatility.
  - Heightened exposure to public health crises (e.g., COVID-19) and related governmental/industry responses.
  - Regional economic and political instability and broader geopolitical risks.
- Failure to manage these challenges could undermine the success of global expansion and limit overall business growth.

nodes.title: Any acquisitions, strategic investments, entries into new businesses, joint ventures, divestitures, and other transactions could fail to achieve strategic objectives, disrupt our ongoing operations or result in operating difficulties, liabilities and expenses, harm our business, and negatively impact our results of operations.
nodes.heading: 1.2.10 Any acquisitions, strategic investments, entries into new businesses, joint ventures, divestitures, and other transactions could fail to achieve strategic objectives, disrupt our ongoing operations or result in operating difficulties, liabilities and expenses, harm our business, and negatively impact our results of operations.
nodes.start_phrase: In pursuing our business strategy, we routinely conduct discussions and evaluate opportunities for possible acquisitions, strategic investments, entries into new businesses, joint ventures, divestitures, and other transactions.
nodes.summary:
- The company routinely evaluates and pursues acquisitions, strategic investments, new business entries, joint ventures, divestitures, and related transactions, which can divert management attention, incur costs even if not completed, and may fail to meet strategic objectives.
- Key risks of such transactions include difficulties obtaining regulatory approvals; potential for added regulatory burdens; uncertain returns or revenue uplift; significant acquisition and transition costs; and challenges integrating technology, systems, culture, and personnel.
- Additional risks include failure to realize expected synergies on schedule (or at all); inability to retain key talent; undetected liabilities despite due diligence; compliance gaps at acquired firms (including data privacy and security), compounded by complex technology stacks and technical debt.
- Transactions may hinder entry into new market segments or geographies; jeopardize retention of customers, vendors, and partners; trigger lawsuits or regulatory actions; expose the company to security weaknesses or cyber risks of acquired/partner firms; and result in equity dilution or new debt.
- Divestitures can be difficult to execute on acceptable terms, may be hard to separate operationally, can reduce revenue or margins, and might not yield intended strategic or financial benefits.
- Example: Sale of Caviar to DoorDash created exposure to mark-to-market volatility of DoorDash equity, lock-up constraints on selling shares, potential failure to realize value, and ongoing liabilities (including indemnities) and relationship disruptions.
- During divestiture processes, businesses may decline, and employees, customers, or suppliers may be lost; deals may fail to close, leaving sunk costs and uncertainty about finding equivalent buyers.
- Joint ventures and minority investments entail reduced control, higher financial/legal/operational/regulatory risks, dependence on partners with potentially conflicting interests, and potential for actions that harm investment value, invite litigation/regulatory action, or damage brand reputation.
- Square Capital faces specific risks tied to third-party investor demand for loans originated by its bank partner; reduced purchases or pricing/servicing-fee cuts could force scaling back, require company funding, and harm performance; repurchase obligations exist for eligibility breaches.
- Square Capital loans are unsecured; macroeconomic deterioration or weaker seller credit can increase defaults, extend repayment periods, and reduce servicing fees; recourse is limited to the business.
- COVID-19 has heightened risks by reducing eligible sellers, complicating seller identification and risk management for the bank partner, increasing expected losses on owned loans, and elevating non-payment and fraud risks.

nodes.title: Square Capital is subject to additional risks relating to the availability of capital, seller payments, availability and structure of its bank partnership, expansion of its products, regulatory obligations, and general macroeconomic conditions.
nodes.heading: 1.2.11 Square Capital is subject to additional risks relating to the availability of capital, seller payments, availability and structure of its bank partnership, expansion of its products, regulatory obligations, and general macroeconomic conditions.
nodes.start_phrase: Square Capital, which includes our wholly owned subsidiary Square Capital, LLC, is subject to risks in addition to those described elsewhere in this Annual Report on Form 10-K.
nodes.summary:
- Risks from acquisitions and divestitures: potential equity dilution, new debt, difficulty selling assets on acceptable terms, separation and integration challenges, loss of revenue/margins, and failure to realize strategic/financial benefits. Example: 2019 sale of Caviar to DoorDash created mark-to-market volatility tied to DoorDash’s stock and lock-up constraints, with no assurance of realizing full value. Transactions can delay objectives, add costs, disrupt relationships, and create ongoing obligations (including indemnities). Pending divestitures risk business decline, loss of employees/customers/suppliers, failure to close, and sunk costs.
- Joint ventures and minority investments: reduced control heightens financial, legal, operational, regulatory, and compliance risks; dependence on partners or controlling parties with potentially conflicting goals; partners’ actions can impair investment value, trigger litigation/regulatory action, and harm reputation/brand.
- Square Capital risks: dependence on institutional investors to purchase bank-originated business loans; if investor demand, pricing, or servicing fees fall, originations may drop or the company may need to self-fund or scale back; repurchase obligations for eligibility breaches. Loans are generally unsecured; adverse macroeconomic conditions (including COVID-19) and seller credit deterioration can increase defaults, extend repayment, and reduce servicing fees; elevated losses on owned portfolio. Lending paused (except PPP) in Q2 2020 and resumed in Q3 under stricter criteria with uncertain volumes; underwriting/pricing misestimation could materially harm the business.
- Bank partnership and regulatory exposure: non-exclusive partnership with a Utah-chartered, FDIC-member industrial bank that may offer competing products; subject to FDIC/Utah oversight and third-party vendor examinations. Ongoing scrutiny and litigation of bank–fintech partnered lending models present risk. Loss or unfavorable change of the bank partner, or inability to secure alternatives/state licenses, could be costly, delay operations, reduce investor participation, and adversely affect Square Capital.
- Future models and licensing: exploring additional products/structures, including forming a Utah industrial bank and other credit offerings, which may require new data, procedures, partnerships, licenses, and regulatory approvals; state licensing entails reporting, bonding, and inspections. Failure to expand/evolve successfully or burdensome regulations could impede growth and success of Square Capital.
- Operational/data security risks: the company, sellers, and partners handle large volumes of sensitive data (PII, payment details, bank info, loan data, seller performance), with certain products subject to HIPAA. Reliance on third-party developers, vendors, and a distributed workforce increases exposure. Breaches, ransomware/APT attacks, or bugs—actual or perceived—could lead to unauthorized access or exfiltration of data/funds, damage brand and business, and result in material costs and liabilities.

nodes.title: Operational Risks
nodes.heading: 1.3 Operational Risks
nodes.start_phrase: We, our sellers, and our partners, including third-party vendors and data centers that we use, obtain and process large amounts of sensitive data, including data related to our customers, our sellers’ customers, and their transactions.
nodes.summary:
- Square Capital paused new business loans (except PPP) in Q2 2020 due to pandemic impacts, then resumed in Q3 2020 with stricter eligibility; future loan volumes remain uncertain.
- Misjudging borrower repayment likelihood or mispricing loans could materially and adversely affect the business.
- Lending is conducted via a non-exclusive partnership with a Utah-chartered, FDIC-member industrial bank that may also offer competing products.
- As a third-party service provider to the bank, the company is subject to FDIC vendor audit standards and examinations, as well as Utah state oversight.
- There is ongoing regulatory scrutiny and potential litigation of bank–fintech partnered lending models, especially where loans are originated by a bank and then sold to a non-bank that helps originate/service them.
- If the bank partner exits, changes terms, or cannot partner on reasonable terms—and suitable alternatives or state-licensed self-origination are not secured—Square Capital may face delays, higher costs, loss of institutional loan buyers, and material adverse impacts.
- The company is exploring additional products and structures, including forming a Utah industrial bank and other credit offerings, which may require new data capabilities, procedures, partnerships, licenses, and regulatory approvals; failure to obtain these or adapt to new rules could hinder growth.
- Operational risks include extensive handling of sensitive data (PII, payment, banking, loan, business performance, and certain HIPAA-protected health information), reliance on third-party vendors and a distributed workforce, and exposure through third-party apps on Square and Weebly marketplaces; breaches, ransomware/APT attacks, or perceived incidents could compromise data, harm reputation, and materially affect the business.

nodes.title: We, our sellers, our partners, and others who use our services obtain and process a large amount of sensitive data. Any real or perceived improper or unauthorized use of, disclosure of, or access to such data could harm our reputation as a trusted brand, as well as have a material and adverse effect on our business.

nodes.start_phrase: We, our sellers, and our partners, including third-party vendors and data centers that we use, obtain and process large amounts of sensitive data, including data related to our customers, our sellers’ customers, and their transactions.
nodes.summary:
- Square Capital paused regular business lending in Q2 2020 except PPP loans; resumed in Q3 2020 with stricter criteria, with uncertainty around future volumes and credit performance.
- Mispricing or misjudging repayment risk on business loans could materially harm results.
- Lending is originated through a non-exclusive partnership with a Utah-chartered, FDIC-member industrial bank that may also compete with the company; the company is subject to FDIC third-party vendor audits and oversight.
- Partnered-lending models face regulatory scrutiny and litigation risk; loss or deterioration of the bank partnership, or inability to secure alternatives or state licenses, could disrupt lending and deter institutional loan buyers.
- The company may explore new structures, including forming a Utah industrial bank and launching new credit/loan products, which could require additional data, processes, partnerships, licenses, and regulatory approvals; state licensing brings reporting, bonding, and inspections.
- Failure to successfully expand Square Capital or comply with evolving regulations could adversely affect growth and performance.
- Significant operational risks from handling large volumes of sensitive data (PII, financial, loan, and, for some products, HIPAA-regulated health data) across the company, sellers, partners, vendors, and a distributed workforce.
- Exposure to third-party developer apps increases data access risks; breaches, ransomware/APT attacks, or perceived incidents could cause reputational damage, remediation costs, litigation, and regulatory actions.
- Liability under payment card rules for card data breaches by the company, sellers, or third parties; breaches of bitcoin/blockchain ecosystems could also erode trust.
- Cyber insurance may be inadequate or unavailable; large uncovered claims could materially impact financials.
- Risks of software/hardware defects, system errors, security issues, and human error affecting high-volume, complex transaction processing; potential settlement errors, reporting issues, and fee collection impacts.
- Reliance on a limited number of overseas hardware suppliers reduces quality control; defects can trigger recalls, shortages, redesigns, investigations, and lawsuits.

nodes.title: Our products and services may not function as intended due to errors in our software, hardware, and systems, product defects, or due to security breaches or human error in administering these systems, which could materially and adversely affect our business.
nodes.heading: 1.3.2 Our products and services may not function as intended due to errors in our software, hardware, and systems, product defects, or due to security breaches or human error in administering these systems, which could materially and adversely affect our business.
nodes.start_phrase: Our software, hardware, systems, and processes may contain undetected errors or vulnerabilities that could have a material adverse effect on our business, particularly to the extent such errors or vulnerabilities are not detected and remedied quickly.
nodes.summary:
- Cybersecurity and data breach risks: Potential for significant financial losses, remediation costs, legal liability, regulatory scrutiny, and investigations; exposure under payment card rules if seller or third-party breaches occur; reputational damage that can hinder customer acquisition and retention; third-party and ecosystem breaches (including bitcoin/blockchain) can have similar reputational effects; cyber insurance may be inadequate or denied, and large claims could exceed coverage.
- Product and service reliability risks: Undetected errors or vulnerabilities in software, hardware, and systems; defects found in customer-facing software/hardware and third-party integrations; reliance on a limited set of overseas suppliers reduces control over product quality; growing complexity and acquisitions increase risk; frequent updates heighten the chance of errors.
- Operational and financial impacts of errors/security incidents: Possible payment settlement delays or errors, oversettlement, reporting mistakes, and loss of transaction fees; unauthorized access to sensitive or confidential data; product safety issues in hardware that could trigger recalls, shortages, redesign costs, regulatory inquiries, litigation, and other liabilities.
- Targeted cyber-attacks: Electronic payment, hardware, and software products are frequent targets; attack techniques evolve rapidly and may be hard to detect or prevent; failure to anticipate or block attacks can harm customers, reputation, and create significant liability.
- System outages and catastrophic event risks: Service interruptions can arise from cyber-attacks, human error, natural disasters, power/telecom failures, pandemics, and geopolitical unrest affecting company and third-party data centers; limited redundancy and disaster recovery not sufficient for all scenarios; heightened regulatory scrutiny of business continuity and disaster recovery for financial services; denial-of-service and other incidents have occurred and likely will continue, causing revenue loss and remediation costs; COVID-19 increased attack surface due to remote work and digital activity; persistent outages can drive customers to competitors and prompt damage claims.
- Geographic and insurance exposure: Headquarters and some data centers in the earthquake-prone San Francisco Bay Area; insurance may not cover significant losses from service disruptions or disasters, potentially leading to material adverse impacts.
- Bitcoin custody risks: Loss, destruction, or compromise of private keys could render bitcoins inaccessible; wallets may be hacked or compromised; inability to access customer-held bitcoins would harm customer trust and the company’s reputation.

nodes.title: Systems failures, interruptions, delays in service, catastrophic events, and resulting interruptions in the availability of our products or services, or those of our sellers, could harm our business and our brand, and subject us to substantial liability.
nodes.heading: 1.3.3 Systems failures, interruptions, delays in service, catastrophic events, and resulting interruptions in the availability of our products or services, or those of our sellers, could harm our business and our brand, and subject us to substantial liability.
nodes.start_phrase: Our systems and those of our third-party vendors, including data center facilities, may experience service interruptions, outages, cyber-attacks and security incidents, human error, earthquakes, hurricanes,
nodes.summary:
- Heightened cybersecurity risks to electronic payment, hardware, and software products, with evolving attack techniques that are hard to detect or prevent, potentially harming customers, damaging reputation, and creating significant liability.
- Vulnerability to system failures and service interruptions from outages, cyber-attacks, human error, natural disasters, power/telecom disruptions, fraud, geopolitical events, regulatory changes, and physical security incidents (break-ins, sabotage, vandalism).
- Limited system redundancy and disaster-recovery preparedness; increased regulatory scrutiny for business continuity and disaster recovery plans that can be costly and resource-intensive.
- Ongoing exposure to denial-of-service attacks and other incidents leading to revenue loss, repair/remediation costs, and data loss or corruption.
- COVID-19-driven increase in cyber risks due to remote work and growth in online payments and commerce; prolonged or frequent service degradation could cause customer attrition and lasting reputational damage.
- Potential legal claims from customers and counterparties arising from outages or failures, with associated time and cost burdens even if claims are unsuccessful.
- Significant natural or man-made disaster risk, particularly given headquarters and data centers in the seismically active San Francisco Bay Area; possible lengthy service interruptions, related liabilities, and insufficient insurance coverage.
- Adverse impacts on sellers and customers from widespread disasters or pandemics that could negatively affect overall operating results.
- Bitcoin custody risk: loss, destruction, or compromise of private keys (without accessible backup) could render bitcoins inaccessible; risk of wallet hacks; potential harm to customer trust and business.

nodes.title: The loss or destruction of a private key required to access our bitcoin may be irreversible. If we are unable to access our private keys or if we experience a hack or other data loss relating to the bitcoins we hold on behalf of customers, our customers may be unable to access their bitcoins and it could harm customer trust in us and our products.
