If we are unable to access our private keys or if we experience a hack or other data loss relating to the bitcoins we hold on behalf of customers, our customers may be unable to access their bitcoins and it could harm customer trust in us and our products.
nodes.start_phrase: Bitcoins are controllable only by the possessor of both the unique public key and private key relating to the local or online digital wallet in which the bitcoins are held.
nodes.summary:
- Escalating cybersecurity threats to electronic payment, hardware, and software products, with evolving attack techniques that are hard to detect and prevent, risking customer harm, reputational damage, and significant liability.
- Systems resilience risks: service interruptions and outages from cyber-attacks, human error, vendor/data center failures, power/telecom disruptions, natural disasters, pandemics, and geopolitical events; some systems lack full redundancy and disaster recovery may be insufficient.
- Heightened regulatory scrutiny for business continuity and disaster recovery in financial services, increasing costs and diverting resources.
- Ongoing DDoS and other cyber incidents have caused and may continue to cause revenue loss, remediation expenses, and data loss/corruption; COVID-19 has expanded attack surfaces via remote work and increased online activity.
- Prolonged or frequent product/service interruptions can drive customer churn to competitors, damage brand trust, and trigger costly, time-consuming claims and litigation.
- Concentration risk from natural or man-made disasters, particularly seismic risk in the San Francisco Bay Area where headquarters and data centers are located; insurance may be insufficient to cover significant service disruption losses.
- Bitcoin custody and private key risks: loss, destruction, or compromise of private keys (or wallet hacks) could irreversibly block access to customer bitcoins, erode trust, require significant remediation spend, and expose the company to litigation and liability; broader crypto ecosystem breaches can also harm reputation; growing bitcoin balances amplify consequences.
- Potential ineffectiveness of risk management programs to vet customers and transactions, with exposure to fraud, scams, money laundering, and terrorist financing, especially given highly automated/liquid payment and P2P services.
- Scaling, product expansion (e.g., online acceptance, consumer financing, loans), and entry into new markets increase difficulty forecasting fraud losses and setting reserves; COVID-19 and growth place additional strain on compliance and risk infrastructure.
- Insurance coverage gaps and selective self-insurance may leave the company exposed to certain risks and expenses.
- Chargeback and refund exposure: higher risk for sellers with future delivery obligations and during economic downturns; inability to recover from insolvent or closed sellers results in losses borne by the company as merchant of record; limited reserves may not fully mitigate losses.
- EMV liability shift increases seller responsibility for certain fraud when not using EMV-compliant readers; not all offered readers are EMV-compliant, raising reimbursement needs and the risk of fines or penalties from payment networks if chargeback losses exceed acceptable levels.

nodes.title: Our risk management efforts may not be effective, which could expose us to losses and liability and otherwise harm our business.
nodes.heading: 1.3.5 Our risk management efforts may not be effective, which could expose us to losses and liability and otherwise harm our business.
nodes.start_phrase: We offer payments and other products and services to a large number of customers.
nodes.summary:
- Security risks related to cryptocurrencies and blockchain: potential hacks, loss of private keys, and compromises of digital wallets (both customer and third-party) could block access to funds, damage trust, trigger remediation costs and litigation, and create reputational harm; risk grows as customer bitcoin balances increase.
- Limitations of risk management: challenges in detecting and preventing fraud and illegitimate transactions; increased exposure from larger sellers; potential regulatory enforcement and partner contract breaches; susceptibility of payments and peer-to-peer services to scams, identity theft, money laundering, and terrorist financing; need for ongoing enhancement amid COVID-19 impacts and expansion; difficulty forecasting losses for new services/markets; partial reliance on self-insurance and limited insurance coverage.
- Chargeback and refund exposure: higher risk with future-delivery sellers and during economic downturns; insolvency or bankruptcy of sellers can shift losses to the company as merchant of record; limited reserves may not cover losses; EMV liability shift increases reimbursement demands on non-EMV sellers; potential fines, higher fees, or loss of card-processing ability if chargeback losses are not controlled.
- Dependence on payment card networks and acquiring processors: reliance on Visa, MasterCard, American Express, Discover, and third-party banks/processors; risks from contract expirations, unfavorable renewals, service degradation, or preferential treatment for competitors; mandatory compliance with evolving network operating rules (including payment facilitator rules) with potential fines or processing bans for violations; possible loss of incentives and increased costs.
- Fee and pricing risks: obligation to pay interchange, assessments, processing, and settlement fees that networks may increase or regulators may alter; favorable pricing often contingent on business conditions; standard-rate pricing model exposes margins and competitiveness to fee changes; peer-to-peer costs could rise if network fees increase.
- Penalties for high-risk or illegal seller activity: responsibility to prevent or register and monitor high-risk sellers; failure can result in material penalties, required onboarding process changes, or termination of card acceptance.

nodes.title: We are dependent on payment card networks and acquiring processors, and any changes to their rules or practices could harm our business.
nodes.heading: 1.3.6 We are dependent on payment card networks and acquiring processors, and any changes to their rules or practices could harm our business.
nodes.start_phrase: Our business depends on our ability to accept credit and debit cards, and this ability is provided by the payment card networks, including Visa, MasterCard, American Express, and Discover.
nodes.summary:
- The company’s business depends on accepting credit and debit cards via payment card networks (Visa, Mastercard, American Express, Discover) and third‑party banks/acquiring processors; disruptions, unfavorable renewals, or preferential treatment of competitors by these partners could harm operations.
- Acquiring processor agreements are time‑limited (major ones expiring between Q3 2022 and Q1 2023), and counterparties could refuse to process transactions adequately, breach terms, or impose added costs/requirements.
- Payment card networks can change or reinterpret operating rules at any time, including payment facilitator rules and chargeback standards; noncompliance can lead to fines, loss of incentives, increased costs, mandated operational changes, or termination of card acceptance.
- Rising interchange, assessment, processing, and bank settlement fees—whether from network decisions, missed pricing conditions, or regulation—could compress margins, force pricing model changes, or reduce competitiveness, particularly because seller pricing often does not pass through these fees directly; similar fee increases could affect peer‑to‑peer transactions on Cash App.
- Ineffective risk management (e.g., self‑insurance, seller reserves) could lead to significant financial losses and potential civil or criminal liability.
- Failure to detect or properly manage high‑risk or illegal seller activity can trigger network penalties, require enhanced monitoring/registration of such sellers, and potentially jeopardize the ability to accept payment cards.
- Overall, any material limitations on card acceptance or increases in transaction‑based fees would adversely affect the company’s business and financial results.

nodes.title: We rely on third parties and their systems for a variety of services, including the processing of transaction data and settlement of funds to us and our sellers, and these third parties’ failure to perform these services adequately could materially and adversely affect our business.
nodes.heading: 1.3.7 We rely on third parties and their systems for a variety of services, including the processing of transaction data and settlement of funds to us and our sellers, and these third parties’ failure to perform these services adequately could materially and adversely affect our business.
nodes.start_phrase: To provide our products and services, we rely on third parties that we do not control, such as the payment card networks, our acquiring and issuing processors, the payment card issuers, a carrying broker, various financial institution partners, systems like the Federal Reserve Automated Clearing House, and other partners.
nodes.summary:
- Heavy reliance on third-party financial networks and partners (payment card networks, acquiring/issuing processors, card issuers, brokers, banks, and ACH/Fed systems) for core services like transaction transmission, chargebacks/refunds, settlements, and brokerage; a limited set of acquiring processors by region increases concentration risk.
- Operational and financial exposure if these third parties experience outages, errors, insolvency, or impose unfavorable terms; switching providers could be costly and disruptive. The company has previously experienced third-party outages that affected branded card processing.
- Dependence on key executives and skilled employees; loss of leadership or key personnel could disrupt operations. Jack Dorsey’s dual CEO role may constrain his availability.
- Intense competition for talent, especially in the San Francisco Bay Area, may require significant cash and equity to attract/retain employees; immigration policy changes could hinder hiring and international operations.
- Need to continually enhance infrastructure, internal controls, and reporting to manage growth and new business lines; priorities include upgrading administrative systems, installing stronger management information and control systems, and preserving and communicating core values and strategies globally.
- Failure to recruit/retain talent or to improve operational and financial systems could materially harm business performance and growth prospects.

nodes.title: We depend on key management, as well as our experienced and capable employees, and any failure to attract, motivate, and retain our employees could harm our ability to maintain and grow our business.
nodes.heading: 1.3.8 We depend on key management, as well as our experienced and capable employees, and any failure to attract, motivate, and retain our employees could harm our ability to maintain and grow our business.
nodes.start_phrase: Our future success is significantly dependent upon the continued service of our executives and other key employees.
nodes.summary:
- Dependence on third-party providers: The company relies on payment networks, acquiring and issuing processors, card issuers, a carrying broker, financial institution partners, and systems like the Federal Reserve ACH for core functions such as transaction transmission, chargebacks/refunds, fund settlement, brokerage, and data services. Transitioning providers could be disruptive and costly. Failures, outages, errors, insolvency, or unfavorable terms from these third parties could materially and adversely affect operations; the company has experienced third‑party outages impacting branded card payments.
- Concentration of acquiring processors: Relies on three acquiring processors in the U.S., Canada, and Japan, and two in Australia and the U.K., heightening transition and continuity risks.
- Talent and leadership risks: Success depends on retaining executives and key employees; loss of such personnel could disrupt operations and increase costs. The CEO’s concurrent role at another company may limit time and focus. Recruiting and retaining highly skilled talent is competitive and costly, especially in the San Francisco Bay Area, and returns on such investments are uncertain.
- Immigration and global staffing constraints: Potential changes to U.S. and other countries’ immigration/visa policies may hinder hiring, renewals, or project staffing, adversely affecting international expansion and overall operations.
- Scaling and internal controls: Rapid growth and new business lines place significant demands on management and resources. The company must strengthen infrastructure, operational procedures, internal controls, and reporting systems to manage growth effectively. Key challenges include improving administrative infrastructure (operational, financial, communications systems), installing enhanced management information/control systems, and preserving and communicating core values, strategies, and goals across a global workforce.

nodes.title: If we do not continue to improve our operational, financial, and other internal controls and systems to manage growth effectively, our business could be harmed.
nodes.heading: 1.3.9 If we do not continue to improve our operational, financial, and other internal controls and systems to manage growth effectively, our business could be harmed.
nodes.start_phrase: Our current business and anticipated growth, as well as our entry into new lines of business, will continue to place significant demands on our management and other resources.
nodes.summary:
- Heavy reliance on third parties (payment networks, acquiring/issuing processors, card issuers, financial institutions, ACH systems, brokers, app marketplaces) for core services such as transaction transmission, chargebacks/refunds, fund settlement, and brokerage; limited numbers of processors per region increase concentration risk. Failures, outages, errors, unfavorable terms, or insolvency of these partners—and disruptions when adding or switching providers—could materially and adversely affect operations; past third‑party outages have already impacted card processing.

- Dependence on key executives and skilled employees; challenges in attracting, motivating, and retaining talent amid intense competition (especially in the Bay Area), potential immigration/visa constraints, and management transitions. Loss of key leaders (including time commitments of the CEO) or inability to hire/retain talent could disrupt operations, increase costs, and hinder growth and strategic execution.

- Need to scale and strengthen operational, financial, and internal control systems to manage rapid growth and new business lines. Risks include delays in implementing infrastructure and management information systems, difficulty preserving core values and alignment, and reduced agility in launching features and responding to market needs. Failure to implement effective processes and tools could impair competitiveness and business objectives.

- Product interoperability risks: services must work across diverse, third‑party operating systems and browsers; changes by platform owners (including Apple and Google) or app marketplace policies/updates could degrade functionality, add costs, favor competitors, or hinder app distribution and access, negatively impacting usage and customer satisfaction.

- Hardware compatibility risks: readers depend on third‑party mobile device interfaces (e.g., audio jack, Lightning). Changes in device design or connection standards may require costly hardware/software modifications; inability or merchant reluctance to adapt could reduce demand and harm the business.

- Supply chain concentration risks: many key components and manufacturing services are single‑ or limited‑sourced, with limited firm commitments and custom tooling held by manufacturers. Exposure to shortages, long lead times, price increases, tariffs, design changes, delays, or discontinuations may disrupt production. Alternative supplier qualification efforts may not succeed, which could materially and adversely affect product availability and costs.

nodes.title: Our services must integrate with a variety of operating systems, and the hardware that enables merchants to accept payment cards must interoperate with third-party mobile devices utilizing those operating systems. If we are unable to ensure that our services or hardware interoperate with such operating systems and devices, our business may be materially and adversely affected.
nodes.heading: 1.3.10 Our services must integrate with a variety of operating systems, and the hardware that enables merchants to accept payment cards must interoperate with third-party mobile devices utilizing those operating systems. If we are unable to ensure that our services or hardware interoperate with such operating systems and devices, our business may be materially and adversely affected.
nodes.start_phrase: We are dependent on the ability of our products and services to integrate with a variety of operating systems, as well as web browsers, that we do not control.
nodes.summary:
- Growth and operational scalability risk: The company must develop robust processes and tools to manage a growing enterprise, requiring significant investments. Balancing added controls with rapid feature development may slow innovation relative to smaller competitors. Failure to effectively manage growth could impair business performance.

- Dependence on third-party platforms and ecosystems: Products and services must interoperate with multiple operating systems, web browsers, and third-party mobile devices. Changes by platform owners (e.g., Apple, Google) or their app marketplaces—such as policy shifts, software updates, or preferential treatment of competing services—can degrade functionality, increase costs, reduce accessibility, and harm usage.

- Hardware compatibility challenges: Company hardware relies on device interfaces (e.g., audio jack, Lightning). Changes in connectors or device designs may require costly modifications or additional parts, and merchant reluctance to adopt such changes could adversely affect the business.

- Concentrated supply chain exposure: Many key components and manufacturing services are single- or limited-sourced, with some reliance on a single manufacturer for assembly and custom-tooled parts. Agreements often auto-renew but lack firm commitments on volumes or timelines. This creates risks of shortages, delays, price increases, tariffs, or discontinuations, and efforts to qualify alternative suppliers may not succeed.

- Overall impact: Any of these factors could materially and adversely affect product performance, customer satisfaction, and the company’s business.

nodes.title: Many of our key components are procured from a single or limited number of suppliers. Thus, we are at risk of shortage, price increases, tariffs, changes, delay, or discontinuation of key components, which could disrupt and materially and adversely affect our business.
nodes.heading: 1.3.11 Many of our key components are procured from a single or limited number of suppliers. Thus, we are at risk of shortage, price increases, tariffs, changes, delay, or discontinuation of key components, which could disrupt and materially and adversely affect our business.
nodes.start_phrase: Many of the key components used to manufacture our products, such as the custom parts of our magstripe reader come from limited or single sources of supply.
nodes.summary:
- Challenges of scaling: Need to implement effective processes, controls, and tools while maintaining agility; risk that growth slows feature delivery and market responsiveness, impairing competitiveness.
- Platform and OS dependencies: Services and hardware must interoperate with multiple operating systems, browsers, and third-party mobile devices; platform changes, added requirements, or preferential treatment of competitors could degrade functionality and demand.
- App marketplace reliance: Dependence on Apple App Store and Google Play; marketplace policy or design changes and software updates can hinder access, break compatibility, reduce downloads, and harm customer satisfaction.
- Hardware interoperability risks: Changes to device interfaces (e.g., audio jack, Lightning) and wireless/wired standards may require costly hardware/software modifications; merchants may resist added accessories, affecting adoption.
- Supplier concentration: Many key components and manufacturing are single- or limited-sourced; limited commitments from contract manufacturers; risk of shortages, long lead times, discontinuations, or price increases.
- Supply chain disruptions: Potential issues from equipment failures, labor shortages/strikes, natural disasters, disease outbreaks (notably COVID-19), cost spikes, insolvency, regulatory changes, trade restrictions, and logistics incidents (e.g., port shutdowns, damage in transit, IP theft, tampering, vendor quality/compliance failures).
- COVID-19 impacts: Ongoing supply chain disruptions, hardware shortages, restricted travel affecting prototype development, and negative effects on seller acquisition and financial results.
- Tariffs and trade policy: U.S. tariffs on China-manufactured hardware (10% rising to 25%, additional 15% later reduced to 7.5%) have pressured gross margins; future tariffs or restrictions could further harm pricing competitiveness and financial performance.
- Demand forecasting and inventory management: Long lead-time investments (e.g., Square Reader) require accurate forecasts; underestimation leads to shortages, overestimation to excess/obsolete inventory, write-downs, discounted sales, and gross margin erosion; demand volatility includes COVID-19-related impacts.
- Overall risk: These factors could materially and adversely affect product availability, customer relationships, growth, profitability, financial condition, and results of operations.

nodes.title: Economic, Financial, and Tax Risks
nodes.heading: 1.4 Economic, Financial, and Tax Risks
nodes.start_phrase: Our performance is subject to economic conditions and their impact on levels of spending by businesses and individuals.
nodes.summary:
- The company faces significant exposure to macroeconomic conditions; downturns reduce spending by small-business sellers (a core customer base), leading to lower payment volumes and adverse financial results.
- Small businesses are disproportionately affected by recessions and the COVID-19 pandemic; closures or reduced activity decrease use of the company’s products and services and can increase transaction and advance loss rates.
- Post-closure chargebacks can create additional losses; growth in and repayment of business loans (e.g., Square Capital) may slow or default; consumers using financing products may also be more vulnerable in downturns.
- Suppliers, distributors, and third-party partners may demand pricing concessions, delay payments, or become insolvent, impairing the company’s ability to meet customer demand and collect revenue.
- The investment portfolio (including U.S. government and corporate securities) is subject to credit, liquidity, market, and interest rate risks; prolonged market declines or downgrades could trigger impairments and hurt financial results.
- COVID-19-related restrictions and ongoing uncertainty may have long-term adverse effects on the economy, customers, suppliers, and the business; remote work and reduced office needs may leave the company paying for unused leased space if subletting is unsuccessful.
- Brexit introduces economic and legal uncertainty and potentially divergent laws, regulations, and licensing requirements, which could negatively affect operations and results.
- Tax risks include exposure to income and non-income taxes across multiple jurisdictions, with audits and disputes potentially leading to higher-than-expected liabilities; an example is a $38 million Texas sales and use tax assessment (2015–2018) that the company disputes regarding the taxability of certain services.

- The investment portfolio faces credit, liquidity, market, and interest rate risks; prolonged market declines or downgrades could trigger impairments and harm financial results.
- Brexit may introduce legal and regulatory divergence in the UK and EU, increasing uncertainty, compliance complexity, and potential operational and financial impacts.
- Significant tax risk exposure: the company is subject to audits and may face disagreements with tax authorities across jurisdictions; example cited is a $38 million Texas sales and use tax assessment that the company disputes, with potential for additional liabilities, interest, and penalties if unsuccessful; reserves may be insufficient.
- Evolving tax laws and practices (including OECD/EU initiatives) could change long-standing principles and broaden taxable activities (e.g., internet hosting, data processing, telecommunications), increasing tax burdens and compliance costs.
- New or expanded taxes (sales & use, VAT, digital services, income) and obligations on marketplaces/payment providers to collect and remit taxes may raise costs, add reporting/record-keeping requirements, and expose the company to penalties and business restrictions for noncompliance.
- Determining global tax provisions is complex and judgment-based; outcomes may differ from estimates and materially affect results.
- The company maintains valuation allowances on deferred tax assets and may adjust them over time; increases or releases could materially impact and cause volatility in quarterly and annual results.

nodes.heading: 1.4.4 We may not be able to secure financing on favorable terms, or at all, to meet our future capital needs, and our existing credit facility contains, and any future debt financing may contain, covenants that impact the operation of our business and pursuit of business opportunities.
nodes.start_phrase: We have funded our operations since inception primarily through debt and equity financings, bank credit facilities, finance lease arrangements, and cash from operations.
nodes.summary:
- Financing risk: Although current cash, marketable securities, and credit availability appear sufficient for working capital, capex, and debt service, the company may need additional capital for opportunities, refinancing, regulatory surety bonds, acquisitions, or unforeseen events and may be unable to obtain financing on favorable terms, in time, or at all, which could constrain growth and responsiveness.

- Debt covenants: The existing credit facility includes affirmative and negative covenants limiting additional debt and liens, intercompany transactions, dividends, and share repurchases; future debt may add further restrictions on capital raising and operations, potentially hindering business execution and acquisitions.

- Default and acceleration risk: Covenant breaches—potentially triggered by factors beyond the company’s control—could cause defaults under the credit facility and other agreements, leading to acceleration of indebtedness, including the 2022, 2023, 2025, 2026, and 2027 Notes.

- Dilution risk: Additional equity or convertible securities could dilute existing stockholders and may carry senior rights, preferences, and privileges relative to Class A common stock.

- Notes servicing and liquidity: Servicing, converting, repurchasing after a fundamental change, or repaying the Notes at maturity may require substantial cash; the company may lack sufficient cash or access to capital when needed.

- Outstanding Notes (as of December 31, 2020): $8.5 million (2022), $862.5 million (2023), $1.0 billion (2025), $575.0 million (2026), and $575.0 million (2027).

- Convertibility status: Before specified dates (Dec 1, 2021 for 2022 Notes; Feb 15, 2023 for 2023 Notes; Dec 1, 2024 for 2025 Notes; Feb 1, 2026 for 2026 Notes; Aug 1, 2027 for 2027 Notes), the Notes are convertible only upon certain conditions. Because the stock price exceeded 130% of the conversion price for the 2022, 2023, and 2025 Notes in Q4 2020, those series are convertible in Q1 2021; future convertibility depends on satisfying similar conditions.

- Settlement approach and EPS impact: Unless settled solely in shares, conversions require cash. Since October 2018, the company expects to settle conversions of the 2022 and 2023 Notes solely in Class A common stock (rather than combination settlement), increasing diluted EPS share count when not anti-dilutive; the policy may be reevaluated upon receipt of conversion notices.

nodes.heading: 1.4.6 We are subject to counterparty risk with respect to the convertible note hedge transactions.

Use of note proceeds may not be optimally productive.
- Legal and default risks: Legal or regulatory limits may restrict repurchases or cash settlements. Failure to meet obligations would constitute a default under the indenture and could trigger cross-defaults under credit facilities and other indebtedness, potentially leading to accelerations the company may be unable to pay.
- Counterparty risk on convertible note hedges: The company entered into hedge transactions with financial institution counterparties; exposure is unsecured and could be impacted by counterparty default or insolvency. Exposure generally increases with the company’s Class A common stock price and volatility. Defaults could cause adverse tax consequences and dilution.
- Bitcoin investment risks and accounting: The company purchased $220 million of bitcoin (Oct 2020 and Feb 2021) and may buy more. Bitcoin’s price is highly volatile and subject to adoption, technological, and security risks. As an indefinite-lived intangible asset, decreases below carrying value trigger impairment charges with no upward revaluation until sale, which can negatively affect reported operating results and financial condition.

nodes.title: Legal, Regulatory, and Compliance Risks
nodes.heading: 1.5 Legal, Regulatory, and Compliance Risks
nodes.start_phrase: We are subject to a wide variety of local, state, federal, and international laws, regulations, licensing schemes, and industry standards in the United States and in other countries in which we operate.
nodes.summary:

- Covered regulatory areas include banking, lending, deposit-taking, money transmission (domestic and cross‑border), foreign exchange, payment services (processing and settlement), cryptocurrency, trading in shares and fractional shares, consumer protection, anti‑money laundering, escheatment, international sanctions, data privacy and security, and PCI DSS compliance.
- Multiple authorities oversee the business: U.S. federal agencies (e.g., FDIC, CFPB), self‑regulatory organizations, state and local bodies (e.g., Utah Department of Financial Institutions), and foreign regulators; expansion into new products or jurisdictions increases this oversight.
- Predicting the applicability and scope of regulations is difficult, especially as offerings and geographies expand, potentially harming current operations and future plans.
- Laws and standards are subject to change and evolving interpretation (including through legislation and executive orders), making compliance planning uncertain.
- Example risk area: the Cash App bitcoin feature operates in an evolving crypto regulatory environment; bitcoin’s volatility, technological and security issues, and regulatory actions pose risks that could lead to enforcement, fines, modification or discontinuation of the feature, and potential negative impact on the company’s stock price.
- The company faces ongoing regulatory inquiries and investigations; despite a compliance program, it may incur fines or penalties from U.S. and foreign regulators, state Attorneys General, and private plaintiffs acting as private attorneys general.
- Potential consequences of non‑compliance include criminal and civil lawsuits, asset forfeiture, heightened licensing requirements, enforcement actions, and mandated changes to business practices and compliance programs.
- Compliance failures or perceived breaches could damage brand reputation, drive customer loss, hinder customer acquisition, and create significant remediation costs and legal liabilities.
- Reliance on third‑party partners and intermediaries introduces additional risk, including potential liability for their corrupt or illegal acts (e.g., in dealings with government officials or state‑affiliated entities), despite internal policies and procedures intended to ensure compliance.

nodes.heading: 1.5.2 Our business is subject to complex and evolving regulations and oversight related to privacy and data protection.

nodes.summary:

The company relies on EU model contractual clauses for transfers but faces added obligations and uncertainty following the CJEU’s Schrems II decision invalidating the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield, potentially increasing compliance costs and operational limits.

- In the U.S., the CCPA and CPRA impose strict requirements and penalties (up to $7,500 per violation), with ongoing uncertainty in interpretation and enforcement; additional state and potential federal privacy laws are emerging, with evolving interpretations that may necessitate policy and practice changes.
- The company has incurred and may continue to incur significant costs to comply with laws, industry standards, consumer expectations, and contractual obligations; failure or perceived failure to comply could reduce customer usage, disrupt partners and supply chains, and materially harm the business.
- As a licensed money transmitter, the company holds licenses in the U.S. and certain non-U.S. jurisdictions (including the EU, U.K., and Australia) and is subject to obligations and restrictions related to customer fund investment, reporting, bonding, and regulatory inspections.

structure.heading: Item 7. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
structure.start_phrase:
You

 financial statements and the notes thereto included elsewhere in this Annual Report on Form 10-K.
structure.summary:
- Context and caution: MD&A with forward-looking statements to be read alongside financial statements and risk factors.
- Business overview: Square’s two ecosystems—Seller (commerce tools, hardware, software, financial services) and Cash App (store, send, spend, invest)—their products, monetization models, and global footprint.
- Segments: Shift to two reportable segments (Seller and Cash App) effective June 30, 2020, reflecting internal performance management.
- COVID-19 impact: Early 2020 GPV decline due to lockdowns; recovery with relaxation of restrictions; shift to higher-priced card-not-present transactions; increased Cash App engagement from stimulus and unemployment deposits; ongoing monitoring of transaction/loan losses and asset impairments (no impairments as of 12/31/20).
- PPP participation and liquidity support: Licensed for PPP lending (facilitated $857M in 2020; $399M sold; forgiveness activity; second-round participation in Feb 2021). Entered PPPLF with the Federal Reserve ($464.1M outstanding at 12/31/20; expanded capacity in Jan 2021).
- Capital markets activity: Issued $1.0B 2025 notes (0.125%); $575M 2026 notes (0%); $575M 2027 notes (0.25%) for general corporate purposes; existing 2022 and 2023 notes outstanding.
- Revenue components: Definitions and drivers of transaction-based; subscription and services (Cash App Instant Deposit, Cash Card, Square Capital, Instant Transfers, software subscriptions); hardware; and bitcoin (recorded gross; small margin; demand and price-driven).
- Cost of revenue and margins: Transaction fees to third parties; Cash App and Instant Transfer costs; hardware sold primarily to drive ecosystem adoption; bitcoin costs mirror revenue; amortization of acquired tech.
- Operating expenses: Product development (personnel, infrastructure, tooling); sales and marketing (advertising, Cash App incentives/processing, card issuance); general and administrative (support functions, professional fees); transaction and loan losses (chargebacks, COVID-related estimates); amortization of acquired customer assets; 2019 gain on sale of Caviar.
- 2020 vs. 2019 results:
  - Total net revenue up 101% to $9.50B; ex-bitcoin up 17%.
  - Transaction-based revenue up 7% aligned with 6% GPV growth; mix shift to card-not-present and pricing changes aided results.
  - Subscription and services revenue up 49% (ex-Caviar +74%) driven by Cash App, Square Card, and Instant Transfers; Square Capital volumes down and temporarily paused (other than PPP).
  - Hardware revenue up 8% (international and contactless hardware promotions).
  - Bitcoin revenue up 785% to $4.57B, but bitcoin gross profit only 3.5% of total gross profit.
  - Cost of revenue up 140% driven by bitcoin; ex-bitcoin down ~1% with lower transaction-based costs due to debit mix and higher average tickets.
  - Operating expenses: Product development +31%; sales and marketing +78% (notably Cash App costs/incentives and advertising); G&A +33%; transaction and loan losses +40% (Cash App growth and COVID reserves).
  - Interest expense rose on new notes; other income driven by gain on DoorDash investment revaluation; 2019 included gain on Caviar sale.
- Segment performance:
  - Seller: Revenue +2%; cost of revenue down 2%; gross profit +8%. Impacts from COVID-19, paused Square Capital lending, higher card-not-present mix and pricing change.
  - Cash App: Revenue +440%; cost of revenue +632%; gross profit +168%. Growth from bitcoin, Instant Deposit, Cash Card, Cash for Business, and stimulus-related direct deposits.
- Quarterly trends and non-GAAP metrics: Eight-quarter tables for revenue mix, costs, operating income, GPV, Adjusted EBITDA, and Adjusted Net Income per Share; noted volatility from COVID-19 and bitcoin; shifting transaction/loan loss reserves through 2020; investment revaluation gains (DoorDash) and prior losses (Eventbrite).
- Liquidity and capital resources: ~$4.9B available funds at year-end; $4.36B in cash, equivalents, restricted cash, and marketable debt securities; $3.0B convertible notes outstanding; undrawn $500M revolver; PPPLF advances outstanding; bitcoin treasury purchases ($50M Oct 2020; $170M Feb 2021) with impairment-only accounting; announced $100M investment initiative for underserved communities; working capital variability drivers (period-end timing, daily GPV).
- Cash flows (2020 vs. 2019): Operating cash flow $382M (net income, non-cash items, PPP loan facilitation timing); investing cash use $607M (securities, capex, acquisitions); financing cash inflow $2.32B (note issuances, PPPLF advances, equity activity).
- Contractual obligations: Schedule of payments for convertible notes (including interest), PPPLF, operating leases, and purchase commitments.
- Critical accounting policies and estimates: Transaction and loan loss reserves (COVID-related revisions and releases), revenue recognition, and convertible notes accounting (debt/equity bifurcation; valuation assumptions).
- Market risk disclosures: Equity price risk from marketable investments (notably DoorDash); non-marketable investment considerations; limited interest rate sensitivity due to short-duration investments; floating-rate exposure if revolver drawn.

structure.title: Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk
structure.heading: Item 7A. Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk
structure.start_phrase:
We
 have operations both within the United States and globally, and we are exposed to market risks in the ordinary course of our business, including theeffects
 of interest rate changes and foreign currency fluctuations.
structure.summary:
- COVID-19 impact on risk estimates: In early 2020 the company increased expected transaction losses (e.g., chargebacks from non-delivery and seller failures). In Q3–Q4 2020, better-than-expected performance led to releasing $82.4 million of previously established risk loss provisions for the first three quarters.
- Convertible notes accounting: Notes are bifurcated into debt and equity components. Debt is measured at the fair value of comparable non-convertible debt; equity equals the residual of principal less the debt fair value. Valuation uses a convertible bond model with subjective inputs (expected term, volatility), involving management judgment and uncertainty.
- Recent accounting pronouncements: Referenced to Note 1 of the consolidated financial statements.
- Market risk overview (Item 7A):
  - Equity price risk—marketable securities: Public equity holdings measured at quoted prices can create earnings volatility. As of Dec 31, 2020, marketable equity investments were $376.3 million with a 2020 gain of $276.3 million; a 10% price move implies about a $37.6 million change, recorded in other expense (income), net.
  - Equity price risk—non-marketable securities: Private investments carry higher inherent risk; changes are recorded in other expense (income), net and reset the carrying value. Carrying value was $32.5 million at Dec 31, 2020; a 10% change would not be material.
  - Interest rate sensitivity: Cash, cash equivalents, and marketable debt securities are primarily short-term (cash deposits, money market funds, U.S. government/agency securities, commercial paper, corporate bonds), limiting sensitivity; instruments can be held to maturity. Any credit facility borrowings would be at floating rates. A 100 bps rate change would not be material.
  - Foreign currency risk: Most revenue is in U.S. dollars, limiting revenue FX exposure. Operating expenses and transactions in JPY, CAD, AUD, EUR, and GBP may create gains/losses; a 10% FX change would not be material.

nodes.title: NOTE 21 - SUBSEQUENT EVENTS
nodes.heading: 1.9.21 NOTE 21 - SUBSEQUENT EVENTS
nodes.start_phrase: On January 28, 2021, the Company entered into a third amendment to the credit agreement for the 2020 Credit Facility to increase the amount ofindebtedness that Square Capital is permitted to incur pursuant to the PPPLF from an aggregate principal amount of up to $500 million to an aggregate principalamount of up to $1.0 billion.
nodes.summary:
- Subsequent events related to financing: On January 28, 2021, the Company amended its 2020 Credit Facility to raise Square Capital’s permitted PPPLF indebtedness limit from $500 million to $1.0 billion.
- PPPLF activity: On January 29, 2021, Square Capital submitted a PPPLF Letter of Agreement to the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco to obtain additional advances secured by second-round PPP loans. As of February 23, 2021, approximately $376.3 million of PPPLF advances were outstanding and fully collateralized by PPP loans.
- PPP participation: In February 2021, Square Capital began participating in the second round of the PPP, accepting applications from certain existing customers who previously received PPP loans through Square Capital. The process was expedited using prior application data; these loans are U.S. government–guaranteed and may be forgiven if criteria are met.
- Digital asset investment: In February 2021, the Company purchased $170 million in bitcoin as a long-term investment and will continue to assess its total bitcoin exposure relative to other investments.
- Accounting matters: No changes in or disagreements with accountants on accounting and financial disclosure.

structure.heading: Item 9A. Controls and Procedures
structure.start_phrase: Our management, with the participation of our Chief Executive Officer and our Chief Financial Officer, has evaluated the effectiveness of our disclosurecontrols and procedures as of the end of the period covered by this Annual Report on Form 10-K.
structure.summary:
- Item 9A—Controls and Procedures: Management, including the CEO and CFO, evaluated the effectiveness of disclosure controls and procedures as of the period end covered by the Form 10-K.
- Definition and scope: Cites Exchange Act Rules 13a-15(e) and 15d-15(e); controls are designed to ensure required information is recorded, processed, summarized, reported timely, and communicated to management for disclosure decisions.
- Assurance level: Management notes controls provide reasonable, not absolute, assurance and involve cost-benefit judgments.
- Conclusion on disclosure controls: CEO and CFO concluded disclosure controls and procedures were effective at a reasonable assurance level as of December 31, 2020.
- Changes in ICFR: Despite a COVID-19-driven shift to remote work beginning March 2020, processes and controls continued to operate effectively; no changes during the quarter ended December 31, 2020 that materially affected or are reasonably likely to materially affect internal control over financial reporting (per Rules 13a-15(d) and 15d-15(d)).
- Management’s ICFR assessment: Management is responsible for ICFR; assessed effectiveness using the COSO 2013 framework and concluded ICFR was effective as of December 31, 2020.
- External audit: Ernst & Young LLP, an independent registered public accounting firm, audited the effectiveness of ICFR as of December 31, 2020, with their report included.
